prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ARM HOLDINGS PLC /UK" (ticker ARM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ARM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Arm Holdings plc
result.industry: Semiconductor intellectual property (CPU architecture licensing) and data center chips
markets: Cloud and AI data center CPUs

mission.statement: Building the future of computing, on Arm. Together. For everyone.
mission.source: 2023 Form F-1 IPO prospectus (presented as Arm's "North Star" statement rather than a formal mission statement)
mission.plain: Arm wants its designs to be the base that computers of every kind are built on, working with partners so everyone can use them.

about.plain: Arm draws the basic blueprints for the 'brain' chips inside computers and phones. It does not usually build the chips itself: other companies pay Arm to use its designs, then pay a small fee for every chip they sell. Almost every smartphone in the world uses an Arm design. In 2026 Arm also started selling its own finished chip for AI data centers.
about.customers: Chip makers and tech giants such as Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung, NVIDIA, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta, plus Arm China.
about.everyday: The processor in nearly every iPhone and Android phone is built on Arm's design.

money.plain: A small fee on every chip sold that uses Arm designs (FY2026: $2,613m of $4,920m)
Up-front fees to use Arm's chip blueprints and tools (FY2026: $2,307m)
Nearly finished, pre-assembled chip designs that earn higher royalty rates
Arm's own finished data center chip, launched March 2026 with Meta as first customer

result.summary: Arm has one of the strongest moats in technology: its instruction set is the standard for smartphones and is spreading to data centers, PCs and cars, and the huge software ecosystem built on it makes switching very costly. Its main risks are the open-source RISC-V alternative, tension with licensees now that Arm sells its own chips, and heavy dependence on China and a few big customers.

pricingPower.evidence: Arm has roughly doubled per-chip royalty rates with the Armv9 architecture and charges more again for Compute Subsystems; royalty revenue rose from $2,168m in FY2025 to $2,613m in FY2026 (+20.5%) even though smartphone unit volumes were roughly flat, and gross margin stayed at 97.5%.

moats.evidence: The Arm instruction set architecture, decades of patents and CPU designs (Cortex, Neoverse) are the industry reference for low-power computing; the brand is well known among engineers though not consumers.
Billions of lines of software, operating systems (iOS, Android) and developer tools are compiled for Arm, so moving a phone or chip line to another architecture means years of rework.
More Arm chips attract more software and developers, which attracts more chip designers; Arm-based chips shipped cumulatively number in the hundreds of billions.
Spreading about $2.8bn of FY2026 R&D across hundreds of licensees lets each customer get a CPU far more cheaply than designing one in-house.
The market supports only a few CPU architectures; outside x86 (Intel/AMD) Arm faces just the emerging RISC-V ecosystem.
The neutral licensing model once made Arm hard to fight, but its move into its own chips (AGI CPU) now puts it in competition with customers, inviting them to consider RISC-V.
35 years of experience making power-efficient CPU cores and working with foundries (TSMC, Samsung) to optimize them is hard to replicate quickly.
Arm owns the Arm architecture outright, so only Arm can grant licences to it; competitors must use x86 (closed) or RISC-V (open).

customers.evidence: Customers stay for decades (Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung, MediaTek); the top five customers were about 57% of FY2026 revenue, but relations with Qualcomm are strained by litigation running since 2022.

talent.evidence: Arm is a respected engineering employer in Cambridge (UK), Austin and Bangalore; stock-based pay since the 2023 IPO helps retention, but it does not appear on major best-places-to-work lists.

product.evidence: Arm cores power Apple's M-series and A-series chips, AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt and NVIDIA Grace, and lead the industry in performance per watt.

competitors.name: RISC-V ecosystem (SiFive)
competitors.note: Open, royalty-free instruction set; SiFive licenses RISC-V CPU cores and wins embedded, automotive and some AI designs

competitors.name: Intel
competitors.note: x86 Xeon server and Core PC processors compete with Arm-based chips; Intel also offers foundry services

competitors.name: Advanced Micro Devices
competitors.note: x86 EPYC server and Ryzen PC CPUs compete with Arm-based Graviton, Axion, Cobalt and the AGI CPU

competitors.name: Qualcomm
competitors.note: Major licensee designing its own Oryon CPU cores (from the Nuvia deal), exploring RISC-V; in litigation with Arm

competitors.name: NVIDIA
competitors.note: Licensee whose Arm-based Grace/Vera CPUs could compete with Arm's own AGI CPU in AI data centers

competitors.name: Andes Technology
competitors.note: Taiwanese RISC-V CPU IP licensor for embedded, automotive and AI chips

competitors.name: Alibaba (T-Head)
competitors.note: XuanTie RISC-V processor IP and chips used in China

competitors.name: Cadence Design Systems
competitors.note: Tensilica processor and DSP IP licensing

competitors.name: Synopsys
competitors.note: Semiconductor interface IP and design tools; formerly ARC processor IP

competitors.name: Imagination Technologies
competitors.note: GPU IP competing with Arm's Mali graphics designs

competitors.name: CEVA
competitors.note: DSP, connectivity and AI accelerator IP for embedded chips

competitors.name: Huawei (HiSilicon)
competitors.note: Develops its own Arm-compatible Kunpeng/Kirin cores, reducing reliance on Arm's designs in China

marketShare.market: Global server shipments by CPU architecture

threats: RISC-V, an open royalty-free architecture, gaining in embedded, automotive, China and possibly data center chips
Selling its own AGI CPU puts Arm in competition with licensees (NVIDIA, Qualcomm, hyperscalers), which could push them toward RISC-V or in-house designs
Qualcomm litigation: Arm lost the Nuvia case (under appeal) and a second trial over Qualcomm's breach claims went to a jury in October 2026
China exposure: about 18% of FY2026 revenue came from the PRC and about 16% from Arm China, an entity Arm does not control, amid US export controls
Customer concentration: the top five customers were about 57% of FY2026 revenue
Big customers (Apple, Qualcomm) designing their own cores reduces the value of Arm's licensing deals
Rising R&D ($2,776m GAAP in FY2026, up 34%) and silicon costs pressuring margins
SoftBank's roughly 90% control limits minority shareholders' influence

ceo.name: Rene Haas
ceo.background: Electrical engineer (BS, Clarkson University); 7 years at NVIDIA running computing products, earlier at Tensilica and Texas Instruments; joined Arm in 2013 and ran its IP Products Group before becoming CEO

c1.evidence: Arm leads the CPU architecture for AI-era computing: about 99% of smartphones run Arm, and Arm-based chips (Graviton, Axion, Cobalt, Grace) are the fastest-growing part of data center CPUs, with IDC estimating 21% of 2025 server shipments.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Arm for performance per watt and a huge software ecosystem spanning Android, iOS, Windows on Arm and Linux; that ecosystem took 35 years to build and is very hard to copy, though RISC-V is a long-term challenger.

c3.evidence: Arm is the default standard among chip engineers, but most ordinary people do not recognise the name even though it is inside nearly every phone they use.

c4.evidence: Arm repeats its 'future of computing is built on Arm' vision and pushes power-efficient AI computing; it is purpose-driven technically, though owned about 90% by SoftBank, whose priorities are financial.

c6.evidence: “power-efficient, everywhere, smartphone chips, AI play, expensive stock” — the impression among people who know it is mostly positive, as the quiet designer inside billions of devices, with debate mainly about its valuation and SoftBank control.

c7.evidence: Arm sells into the whole computing market, which is growing with AI data centers, edge AI on phones and PCs, and software-defined cars.

c8.evidence: Arm is expanding from IP licensing into Compute Subsystems and its own AGI CPU silicon (2026), and from phones into data centers, PCs (Windows on Arm) and automotive.

m1.evidence: Rene Haas laid out a clear picture of Arm moving from licensing to complete subsystems and chips, and of AI running on Arm from the cloud to the edge, and is executing it.

m2.evidence: Haas is not a founder but has served Arm since 2013 and makes bold long-term bets such as the AGI CPU; he works under SoftBank's Masayoshi Son as controlling owner.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way about servant leadership; partners such as Qualcomm have publicly accused Arm of aggressive licensing tactics.

m5.evidence: Under Haas, Arm has moved faster from Armv9 to CSS to its own silicon, but its culture is known more as a steady engineering firm than a distinctive inventive one.

m6.evidence: Haas is an electrical engineer with decades in chip product roles at NVIDIA, Tensilica and Texas Instruments.

m7.evidence: Haas has no notable public controversies, but there is little public evidence of a mission beyond growing Arm's business.

m7b.evidence: I found no record of Rene Haas giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Haas is a capable, low-key industry executive rather than a famous public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2022, revenue rose from $2,703m (FY2022) to $4,920m (FY2026); he led the 2023 IPO and raised royalty rates through Armv9 and CSS.

m10.evidence: Arm is not known for frugality: GAAP R&D grew 34% to $2,776m in FY2026 and stock-based pay is heavy.

c10.evidence: Arm's designs run in billions of phones, tablets, cars and devices each year, so its power-efficient chips make mobile computing possible for most of the world's population.

p2.evidence: Designing leading CPU architectures and the ecosystem around them takes thousands of engineers and decades; it underpins almost every mobile device and a growing share of AI data centers.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew in four of the last five years, from $2,027m (FY2021) to $4,920m (FY2026), but dipped from $2,703m to $2,679m in FY2023.

f2.evidence: Gross margin stays around 95-97.5% (97.5% in FY2026); operating margin rose from 12% in FY2021 to 18.3% in FY2026 but was 25% in FY2023 and only 3.4% in FY2024 because of IPO-related stock pay.

f3.evidence: Arm has no borrowings (only lease liabilities), $3,601m of cash and short-term investments at March 31, 2026, and $8,286m of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $239m (FY2021) to $900m (FY2026) with a dip to $111m in FY2024; operating cash flow was uneven at $1,090m, $397m and $1,524m in FY2024-FY2026.

v1.evidence: For a phone or power-efficient server chip, Arm designs are the default because they deliver more performance per watt (longer battery life, cheaper power bills) and run all the existing software.

v2.evidence: Arm is a respected engineering employer, especially in Cambridge, UK, but it does not appear on major lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If Arm disappeared, almost every phone maker, Apple, Android vendors, cloud providers and carmakers would lose the base design of their chips and years of software work.
